evidence_quotes.quote: With over 100 million people without access to sewage collection and treatment and over 35 million lacking access to piped drinking water, the water and sanitation services (WSS) sector in Brazil ranks last among all the infrastructure sectors.
This paper examines the state of the water and sanitation services in Brazil before 2020 as well as the potential effects of the recently approved reform.

They are: improvements in the regulatory framework; regionalization of the provision of services; standardization of services provision contracts; and removal of barriers to entry to the private sector.
Law 14.026/2020 now requires that any new contract for the provision of services needs to be preceded by a bidding process.
This paper describes the current state of the WSS in Brazil, the new provisions brought about by the reform approved by the Parliament and the potential impact of the reform.
Therefore, the authors of this paper believe that coverage rates will increase at larger rates, but it is unlikely that the goals stated by the law will be reached.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines piped drinking water supply and sewage collection/treatment service coverage and universalization in Brazil.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the paper examines legal, regulatory, and institutional reforms in Brazil's WSS sector (Law 11.445/2007 and Law 14.026/2020). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Law 14.026/2020 directly alters utility ownership/contracting and regulatory structures governing service access, including mandatory competitive bidding to replace non-competitive public/public program contracts, mandatory contract clauses setting 2033 universalization targets (99% water, 90% sanitation), federal funding conditionality to enforce municipal regionalization and regulatory guideline adoption, and ANA standard guidelines on tariff regulation and universal access goals.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (exclude as E05): this BRICS Law Journal article is a descriptive legislative/policy overview and prospective critical commentary on Law 14.026/2020 (enacted July 2020, analyzed as of early 2021). It presents no empirical methodology, no primary data collection, no empirical evaluation of an exposure-outcome relationship, and is not a systematic empirical synthesis; secondary descriptive tables (SNIS 2018/2019, Giambiagi 2021, Juliatto 2020) are cited solely as pre-reform background context.
criterion_notes.c4: Although secondary pre-reform coverage rates from SNIS 2019 are summarized as background context, the paper reports no empirical access outcome resulting from the 2020 legal reform, offering only prospective authorial opinion on whether the 2033 universalization goals will be met.
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, and measured exposure-outcome evaluation because it is a non-empirical legal and policy commentary.

study_design: Non-empirical legal and policy overview / commentary
population_and_sample: No empirical sample; national policy overview of the Brazilian WSS sector citing secondary SNIS descriptive statistics on 5,549 municipalities and 202,214,508 inhabitants
exposure: Law 14.026/2020 (New Basic Sanitation Law) reforming WSS regulatory oversight, regionalization, contract standardization, and competitive bidding rules
outcome: No empirical outcome measured; prospective commentary on potential effects on universal water supply and sewage coverage goals by 2033
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). While the paper addresses household water and sanitation service coverage in Brazil (c1=yes) and analyzes specific statutory and regulatory mechanisms governing service provision under Law 14.026/2020—satisfying both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type readings of Criterion 2 (c2=yes)—it is a non-empirical legal/policy overview and prospective commentary written shortly after the July 2020 enactment of the law. It employs no empirical research design, collects no primary data, conducts no empirical analysis of access outcomes, and is not a systematic empirical synthesis.
